analysis.one_liner: Charges fossil fuel producers a rising fee on carbon pollution and returns the money to households as monthly dividends.
analysis.headline: A climate bill with 95 cosponsors never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a fee on the carbon content of oil, natural gas, and coal, charged to the companies that produce or import them. The fee would start at $15 per metric ton of carbon dioxide and rise by $10 each year, with steeper increases if emissions reductions fall behind schedule. All the money, minus a small administrative share, would go into a Carbon Dividend Trust Fund and be paid out as equal monthly dividends to every adult citizen and lawful resident, with half-shares for children. A border adjustment would charge the same carbon price on imported fuels and goods like steel and cement so domestic producers are not undercut. The bill was referred to three House committees in April 2021 and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Every adult citizen and lawful resident would receive an equal monthly dividend, with half a share per child under 19. Because lower-income households generally burn less fuel than wealthier ones, most low- and middle-income households would come out ahead financially once dividends exceed the higher fuel prices. Households would also benefit from cleaner air and reduced climate damage. Agriculture and the armed forces would be exempt from the fee, and exporters of covered fuels and carbon-intensive products would get refunds so they can compete abroad.

how_it_helps.text: Fossil fuel producers, refiners, and importers pay a fee on every ton of carbon their fuels will emit, starting at $15 per metric ton in 2021 and rising $10 per year, with a $15-per-year escalator if emissions miss reduction targets [S2][S3].

All fee revenue, minus small administrative shares, goes into a Carbon Dividend Trust Fund and is paid monthly to every eligible adult, with half shares for children; the dividend cannot be counted against eligibility for other federal benefit programs [S3].

A carbon border fee adjustment taxes imported fuels and carbon-intensive products like steel, aluminum, and cement at the same rate as domestic fuels, and refunds the fee on exports, protecting U.S. manufacturers from competition with countries that have no carbon price [S3].

Fuels used for farming, by the armed forces, or for non-emitting purposes are exempt or refunded, and facilities that capture and permanently store carbon dioxide get payments equal to the fee they paid [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers, refiners, and importers would pay the fee directly and pass much of it to consumers in higher prices for gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity from fossil sources. Coal, oil, and gas industries would see demand and profits fall as the fee climbs each year. Households that use large amounts of fossil energy could receive a dividend smaller than their added costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and heavy fuel users

drawbacks.text: The fee raises prices for gasoline, home heating, and fossil-generated electricity; households that drive long distances or heat with fuel oil in cold regions could pay more than their dividend, especially in the years before emissions fall [S2][S3].
Dividends are includible in gross income, so recipients would owe income tax on them, slightly reducing the net benefit [S3].

The bill is revenue-neutral by design, so no money is left for direct public investment in clean energy or for compensating workers in coal and oil communities whose industries shrink under the rising fee [S3].

Payments to carbon capture facilities could subsidize continued burning of fossil fuels where capture is incomplete or storage later leaks, an outcome the bill asks the National Academy of Sciences to review after five years [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design directly addresses the main objection to carbon pricing: the dividend returns more money than most households pay in higher energy costs, and the border adjustment protects domestic manufacturers. The serious costs fall on fossil fuel industries and on the minority of households with above-average fossil fuel use, and there is no dedicated support for displaced fossil workers. On balance the policy would shift money from heavy fossil fuel use to ordinary households while cutting emissions, but it never got far enough for the tradeoffs to be tested in legislation.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in three House committees from April 2021 onward and never received a markup or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Theodore Deutch introduced the bill on April 1, 2021 with 29 original cosponsors [S1][S3].
It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and additionally to Energy and Commerce and Foreign Affairs; the next day it was referred to the Energy Subcommittee [S5].
The cosponsor list grew to 95, all Democrats, but the bill never advanced out of committee, received no vote in either chamber, and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1][S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and importers are better off: no carbon fee was ever imposed, and the pre-bill status quo of no federal carbon price continued through the 117th Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers who avoided any carbon fee

for.name: Rep. Theodore E. Deutch
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 1, 2021 and built the largest cosponsor bloc for any carbon pricing bill of that era.

for.name: 95 of 222 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of the 95 were Republicans.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee first on April 1, 2021; no markup or vote ever followed in the 117th Congress.

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee on April 1, 2021 and to its Energy Subcommittee the next day; neither took further action.

against.name: Rep. Gregory Meeks
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee on April 1, 2021 for its trade and treaty provisions; no action followed.

against.name: Fossil fuel industry and allied anti-carbon-tax groups
against.what_they_did: Ran sustained public and lobbying campaigns against carbon tax proposals throughout the period, keeping carbon pricing politically toxic for both parties.

sides.party_line_note: All 95 cosponsors were House Democrats and none were Republicans, and the bill never reached a vote in either chamber, so the split showed up in sponsorship and inaction rather than roll calls.

industries.industry: Coal mining and oil and gas production
industries.note: These industries pay the fee directly on every ton of carbon in their fuels, and the escalating rate is designed to shrink their market over time. Their interest in stopping the bill ran against the dividend and cleaner air the public would receive.
Refineries and importers of petroleum and natural gas are named as covered entities liable for the fee, which they would pass to customers as higher fuel prices.
A rising fossil fuel fee makes renewables, efficiency, and clean technology relatively cheaper, and non-emitting uses of fuels are exempt from the fee.

industries.industry: Carbon-intensive manufacturers (steel, aluminum, cement, chemicals, glass, paper)
industries.note: They would bear higher fuel and energy costs at home, but the carbon border fee adjustment charges imports at the same rate and refunds fees on exports, insulating them from undercutting by countries without carbon pricing.
Farm fuels and military fuel use are exempt or fully rebated, shielding these fuel-heavy sectors from the fee entirely.
